$DIA
 全日沽压最重，收报521.37点，跌1.24%，为三大指数中跌幅最深；标普 SPY 收报759.97点，跌0.52%，失守760关；纳指 QQQ 则在科网股及网络安全股走强带动下靠稳，收报704.40点，微跌0.01%，守住700关之上，表现一枝独秀。中小型股同步偏软，罗素小型股 IWM 收报275.75点，跌0.33%。市宽较指数所反映的更为疲弱——106只观察股中仅45只报升、61只下跌，跌者多于升者，显示指数的相对抗跌主要靠少数权重科网股支撑，大市内部沽压未见收敛。

**板块**｜网络安全及云端板块领涨全场，三线齐飞： CRWD 急升8.25%、 NET 涨7.29%、 PANW 升7.22%，数据平台股 SNOW 亦造好3.65%。能源股逆市靠稳，在油气双雄带动下反复向上， CVX 升2.88%、 XOM 升2.79%，成为防守资金的去向。半导体板块则严重分化， SMTC 升5.50%、通讯设备股 NOK 升3.30%，但AI互联及存储一线重挫， CRDO 暴跌9.51%、 WDC 挫2.97%。消费及零售股普遍受压， TGT 急泻3.38%、 LOW 跌2.78%，汽车股 F 跌2.85%；出行股 UBER 挫3.43%，软件股 ADBE 跌2.49%，医药重磅股 LLY 跌2.54%，加密相关股 COIN 跌2.74%。新兴市场金融股 NU 逆市升2.92%。

**焦点**｜全日最大单一跌幅来自燃料电池股 BE ，大泻11.24%，主因为前一交易日盘后公布的业绩；存储股 WDC 同样于前一交易日盘后交卷，今日收跌2.97%，两者的波动均为财报后的直接反应。至于跌幅榜第二位的 CRDO ，并非财报日,其9.51%的急泻与同属半导体链的 SMTC 升5.50%形成尖锐对照，反映资金并非整体撤离AI硬件,而是在链条内部高度拣择、强弱互换。另一值得注意的是网安三股同日录得逾7%的齐升——在61只下跌的淡市中,这类集体性的板块级跳升,通常意味着板块资金配置的切换,而非个股消息驱动。

**小结**｜全日格局是典型的「指数平稳、内部分化」：纳指近乎平收,道指却跌逾1.2%,旧经济权重与科网龙头的裂口再度扩阔,而市宽（45升61跌）更接近市场的真实温度。分析指,标普失守760关后,此位将由支持转为阻力,而纳指能否守住700关,仍是短线强弱的关键位;若权重科网的升势无法扩散至市宽,目前由少数板块撑起的指数结构将难以持久。与此同时,AI产业链的财富分配问题亦值得留意——本轮周期中最具爆发力的资产大多留在一级市场,公开市场投资者所能拣择的,只剩链条中强弱悬殊的二线标的,这或正是今日 SMTC 与 CRDO 分道扬镳的更深层背景。

AI capex谁出钱这事吵了半年，很少有人把美国财政部算进去。

去年七月那个税法把100%当年折旧改成了永久的。服务器、GPU、交换机这些五年期设备，钱花出去当年就全额抵掉，只有机房壳子慢慢摊。四家大厂一年四千亿美元的capex，就算只按七成是设备、21%的税率算，一年也有五六百亿的税当年不用交。不用申请，没有新闻稿，纯无息贷款。

肯定有人说这只是递延，早晚要还。对，别扭的地方就在这个"早晚"。现在所有人的模型都是capex一降、FCF起飞；可抵扣是跟着当年支出走的，capex降下来那一年，抵扣也跟着没了，cash tax rate会往回跳。你等的那个自由现金流大年，税单正好同一年到。

哪天真开始减capex，我第一眼翻的是现金流量表里cash taxes那一行。

author: Balder13946731
text:
九十年代新竹是真暴富过一波的。台湾那时候有员工配股，公司拿股票当年终奖发，还按面值十块钱算，到手就是几十倍的价差——科学园区满地开BMW的工程师就是这么来的。2008年制度改了，配股要按市价记成本，账上顶不住，整个行业几乎全换成现金分红。

所以今天台积电里做最先进制程的那个人，拿的是薪水加一笔现金奖金，那张会自己涨的纸他拿不到 英伟达那边同期一年发掉四十多亿美元的股票给员工，2015年进去的那批人手上的RSU翻了上百倍。全世界九成的先进制程在台湾做出来，这十年落到做事的人身上的个人财富，其实大部分没在那儿发生，而是在太平洋那一边。

那套能让工程师发财的制度，2008年就关掉了。台积电是后来才慢慢变成地球上最要紧的那家公司的——等它变成的时候，这事已经过去快二十年，没人再提了。

沽压则集中于数字资产相关、消费及医药一端，与大市方向背驰。 CRCL 重挫7.07%；加密货币交易平台 COIN 跌2.95%；经纪商 HOOD 跌2.35%，三者同日失色。流媒体股 NFLX 跌2.96%，药业股 MRK 跌3.21%，零售股 TGT 跌2.77%。拉丁美洲数字银行 NU 单日暴泻16.95%，为全日跌幅最大的观察股，表现与整体升市完全脱节。

**焦点**

盘面以外，市场全日的核心议题仍是算力供给的硬约束。亚马逊管理层表示，AWS 2027年的容量已「基本卖光」。卖光本身是需求强劲的证据，但同时意味着该年度的收入上限不再由需求决定，而是由变压器、涡轮机以及何时通电决定；在全行业同时排队的环境下，工期滑一个季度未必只是递延，客户随时转投手上有现成机位的同业。此一叙事的受益方向，与今日光通讯、网络设备及电力设备股的相对强势一致。

融资端的分化亦值得留意。 META 已递交一份不披露规模的 mixed shelf，先将随时发债发股的额度挂上；与此同时，债券市场对缺乏AI数据中心以外收入来源的发行人态度明显收紧。长端利率高企之下，能够顺利融资的往往是最不缺钱的一批，真正缺钱的反而被关在门外——此为未来AI资本开支叙事的主要风险点。

一级市场方面，Anthropic已递交在纳斯达克上市的申请文件，招股书同时列明其技术对人类构成灾难性、生存层面风险的风险提示。此类表述在法律上属标准免责安排，惟就「生存层面风险」一项而言，其现实约束力有限，料成日后定价争议所在。

能源物流方面，沙特近期在新加坡租用油罐储货，等同在油价仍处高位时主动把现货搬到亚洲买家门口；相同手法十余年前曾在冲绳使用。供应方一边维持掐紧水龙头的叙事，一边替客户修通最后一公里管道，此举对后市原油定价权的含义，值得长线留意。

**小结**

全日为一次由科网及算力硬件主导、市宽配合的普涨，惟升势内部分化鲜明：受益于数据中心基建的光通讯、网络设备与电力设备股明显跑出，而数字资产相关、医药及零售则遭沽压。两只反向杠杆产品的跌幅，确认日内并无明显回吐压力。分析指，后市关键在于 QQQ 能否站稳712水平，以及上升股数能否持续维持在七十只以上；若升势继续由单一板块独力支撑，而市宽转弱，则需提防高位反复偏软。卖方对个别大型科技股的目标价区间分歧已明显扩大，亦反映市场对AI资本开支的盈利路径尚未形成共识。

text:
AI Semis Trade: From Arousal to Reality

The past few weeks have been painful for AI semi investors. One of our mistakes early in the month was not realizing how much of an impact Anthropic’s ARR print would have on the AI trade, and not “sussing” out the set up heading in: lower distillation revs, OpenAI taking share in September, & META/MSFT off-ramps. These were all things that were reported on; if this was an earnings print, we wouldn’t have wanted to be long in the weeks heading into it. In hindsight — knowing what we know now, it was a perfect set up to reduce exposure into it.

The upside of whiffing on that trade and the market’s renewed focus on Lab ARRs and financing? It has forced me (and other investors) to sharpen our pencils and better understand the different moving pieces of the trade, and how they play off each other.

Let’s rewind a bit before diving into where we are now:

For the first three years of the AI semi trade, and especially during the May/June go-go days, investors were in the throes of the honeymoon phase: maximum arousal, minimum scrutiny. Every piece of news was looked at with rose-colored-glasses. It’s just like the beginning of a new relationship when the infatuation is so strong that your partner can do no wrong. Even when she tells you she believes in an "open-source relationship," you somehow hand-wave it away and convince yourself it’s just going to soak up more of the frontier labs' excess demand. When your level-headed friends pull you aside to point out glaring red flags, like the fact that she’s running a shadowy circular-financing scheme with her roommates, you don’t listen; you just stop inviting them to parties. Before you know it, you’ve turned on Gavin Baker’s X notifications and forward SemiAnalysis to anyone who thinks you’re moving too fast, the ultimate wingmen who never stop hyping her up and telling you what you want to hear. “It’s way bigger than just coding, bro. She’s going to replace the entire global labor force.”

Before long, the endorphins and dopamine completely take the wheel. Even if you carry the scars from past relationships — whether the early 2000s, GFC, 2019 SaaS, or the 2020–2022 Covid binge — the blinders go right back on. Those exes weren’t real supercycles and everyone knows there’s no dark fiber in GPUs, you tell yourself as you stare at GPU rental prices. You’ve even picked out baby names: Bel if it’s a girl; Claude if it’s a boy.

But eventually the dopamine wears off, and you have to get to know the person you’ve been telling everyone is perfect. You begin to see the flaws and start asking practical questions about spending habits, expectations, whose money is actually paying the bills. Can we afford this lifestyle on those lab ARRs, or are we just annualizing the honeymoon and assuming the capital stays cheap forever? And is there enough power in ’28 to keep the spark alive?

Things suddenly feel a lot more complicated, and we feel some investors longing for the simpler, more intoxicating days of May and June. But we see the end of the honeymoon as a chance for the relationship to mature. That means accepting where we are, adjusting expectations, and focusing our attention on where the strengths are rather than the flaws...

There’s a really pronounced divide between people who are on the AI side of things and people who are on the biology side of things.  Even among people working in AI, the divide persists based on where they’re focused.

The AI side, adherents of scaling laws and the bitter lesson, believe that AI getting better means AI being more capable of novel discoveries in medicine (that go beyond discovering new drugs in well understood targets or speeding up dry lab work etc). 

The biology people think the idea of a bitter lesson in biology is kind of ridiculous and that regardless of AI’s capabilities it’s going to be at least 5-10 years until you could hope to reliably simulate human toxicology in silico (right now AI/ML can’t even reliably simulate in vivo studies like binding affinities or functional assays). 

Even the most AI pilled of them, who will list all the areas that AI can reduce the time spent on various areas, don’t think the concept of AI discovering novel targets or generating new understanding of causal biology is realistic in the near term. Most, in fact, will readily characterize the assumption that even an “ASI” level model could find cures hidden in our current understanding (without expanding that understanding with significantly more biological data) as patently false. 

This was a big part of why we wanted to experience it ourselves by using AI for a (very) small portion of what it can do in biology. It was both mind blowing and revealed some poignant insights into how different the problem of making AI better at something like coding is to the problems of biology. 

Even if it unlocked the ability to generate new molecules at a stunning pace, its simulation (in silico) of binding only had 49% accuracy. And if we wanted to improve that, we’d need to feed it back the data from the lab - data that took about 30x as long to get as it took to generate the molecules. And these were tests in a test tube (turn of phrase), imagine how long it would take if we wanted to improve the model with data that required recruiting humans and monitoring their reactions. 

Human biology is very complex, and adding a drug - especially a novel drug and doubly so for a novel drug acting on a novel mechanism - means mapping interactions that have nth-order-effects that we don’t have the data to predict. Virtual cells have made advancements enabled by AI, but the perturbations equate to a small fraction of the possible. 

This is before you even get into curing disease, especially uniquely human diseases. Brain function involves cellular identities that are unique to humans, meaning animal studies are of little use. 

How long does it take to understand what the side effects of chronic administration of a drug in humans are? AI can speed up analyzing the data, or designing the trial or even getting it approved…but it can’t make a 6 month trial complete in 3 months. 

I think its important to point out that significant advancements can be made in AI that contribute to biology, while also being realistic about how much it speeds up something as complex as curing a specific cancer or diseases of the brain.

It's been an eventful week. Multiple vulnerabilites in Internet facing software, coding repositories, examples of agent behavior that seem concerning and a flurry of security specialists with solutions that can partially solve your problem. There in lies the challenge. Given the state of IT and security infrastructure, no one solution works. Let's break it down: 
1/3
1. Vulnerabilites are being found and will continue to be found as models get more capable, the fragmented nature of the effort denies us the opportunity for a comprehensive find and replace option. 
2. Even if all vulnerabilities could be found instantly and patches available - we will be reliant on the ability of enterprises to deploy all these changes at speed. It is not clear what the collateral impact of all these patches will/could be to our infrastructure of deployed en masse. 
We will need a hybrid patch approach. 
3. Virtual patching(VP) is needed in conjunction with direct patching  but for a comprehensive (VP) solve you have to be lucky enough to have "modern frontier defenders" (Cyber companies that have vaulted infrastructure that can create patches at speed and push content rapidly to protect their customers) you need them for your network traffic, your traffic to applications on the cloud, your WAF, your end point. 
4. There will continue to be patches that will need to be deployed directly but virtual patching will take the heavy load off. 

2/3 Medium term solve:
 Unfortunately token economics and current cyber architectures will not allow for defender swarms to contend with an offensive attack launched using agents. (Some x pundits who aren't steeped in cyber should take heed). Yes, theoretically we should aspire to have these agentic swarms defend us when we are under attack, unfortunately an attack is a sniper moment, chained vulnerabilities, cloaked attack followed by swift exfiltration. It's a speed program not a brute force problem. 

To solve for this, enterprises need to get their SOC architecture right, logs, feeds, cyber products orchestrated via a modern SOAR for swift response. Only then can we deploy agents to detect and remediate. In addition,  enterprises need to modernize and dare I say platformize  their perimeter stack to ensure consistency. 

Unfortunately, enterprises still seem to not see the urgency across the board, decisions are stuck, CIO/CISO's have a lot on their plate. While some honestly have bit seen the scale of such a problem before and it's hard convincing the organization that one needs to open the floodgates on modernizing the IT and security infrastructure. So we will continue to see environments being brought down to patch today it's for PHP, tomorrow it will be for the next one. 

3/3 AI deployments are the"wild wild west" - LLM capabilities are expanding faster than we can build products to secure them. Sure an agent will jump across guardrails in a research lab, which is a lesson for all of us to deploy agents securely. But there is a lag between the discovery, the availability of that in a public model and the time needed for the cyber industry to build governance or an antidote. And no, dear frontier lab friends, the world cannot just trust you to build the solve. The infrastructure industry in tech builds and the cyber industry secured and provides assurance to the boards and organizations around security and safety. 

AI security is the new attack surface. CEOs (present company included) want AI adoption, getting the pace of adoption wrong could be the last decision we make, at the same time "deploying it wrong" could have the same consequence.

There are billions of dollars being spent on coding, is your coding harness secure? Start there. If agents can jump guardrails, they can hide stuff in code. 

Validate business outcomes needed, test your user case and ensure agentic deployments are well guard railed. Deploy a second set of eyes to watch your deployments for drift, compliance and verifiability.
